entry.title: NATS: The Featherweight Messaging Backbone for Distributed AI

link.title: NATS: The Featherweight Messaging Backbone for Distributed AI

entry.content:
Every serious AI system turns into a fan-out problem embarrassingly fast. One “answer the user” request becomes a burst of calls to an embedding service, a retriever, a reranker, and a model provider; a training run becomes millions of checkpoint, metric, and gradient events; an agent becomes a swarm of workers that need to talk to each other more than they talk to you. Wiring all of that with direct HTTP calls produces a hairball of retries, timeouts, and service discovery. What you actually want is a small, fast post office in the middle: services publish events on subjects, other services subscribe, and nobody keeps a phone book of everyone else’s addresses. That is the niche NATS owns, and unlike heavyweight log brokers such as Kafka, it does so with a single Go binary that will happily run on a Raspberry Pi at the edge of your cluster.

NATS is a CNCF project with a simple pitch: a “simple, secure and performant communications system for digital systems, services and devices,” backed by over 40 client language implementations. The core protocol is text-based and at-most-once — blazing fast fire-and-forget pub/sub with request-reply semantics. On top of that sits JetStream, the built-in persistence layer that turns the same server into a durable, replayable stream store with exactly-once-ish consumer semantics, which makes it a lighter alternative to a dedicated log broker when your durability needs are modest. Security, JWT-based accounts, clustering, gateways, and leaf nodes are all part of the same server, not sidecar plugins.

In this post we read the actual Go source of nats-io/nats-server on the main branch (currently pre-release 2.16.0-dev) and follow a message from a TCP socket to a subscriber — and then to disk, to other servers in a cluster, and to edge nodes. Both diagrams below were generated directly from the repository, so every node links to the real file on GitHub.

NATS at a glance: connections on the left, the subject-trie routing core in the middle, JetStream persistence below, and cluster/edge propagation plus HTTP monitoring on the right.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Server.Start, L2294 — the bootstrap function: it opens the client listener, monitoring server, route accept loop, gateways, leaf node listeners, and JetStream, each in its own goroutine.
  • readLoop, L1503 — one goroutine per connection drains the socket into the parser; the same client struct serves plain clients, routes, gateways, and leaf nodes, differentiated by a kind field.
  • parse, L137 — a hand-rolled state machine that turns raw bytes into OP_CONNECT, OP_PUB, OP_SUB, OP_PING operations without allocating per protocol token.
  • processPub, L3016 — the publish path: validate subject and payload, then hand the message to the fan-out machinery; its sibling processSub, L3121 registers subscriptions.
  • Sublist.Match, L555 — resolution of a subject like orders.*.created against a token trie, with a cache for hot subjects; Insert at L375 maintains the tree.
  • EnableJetStream, L207 — wires the storage directory, system accounts, and encryption keys; once enabled, $JS.API requests are served by apiDispatch, L951.
  • processJetStreamMsg, L6486 — the stream engine’s ingest: de-duplication, retention limits, and a hand-off to the storage backend, where StoreMsg, L5579 appends into on-disk message blocks.
  • connectToRoute, L2933 — how servers find each other: solicited and gossip-discovered routes exchange INFO and sync subscription interest so a publish on one node reaches subscribers everywhere.
  • HandleRoot, L1523 — the monitoring port’s index page, linking the JSON endpoints (/varz, /connz, /jsz, and friends) that operators scrape.

The detailed map: config and lifecycle, the per-connection read loop, interest and auth, the JetStream stack with its storage backends and Raft replication, clustering and edge topology, and the monitoring surface.

From Install to Your First Pub/Sub

NATS is a textbook Go module — the repository root declares module github.com/nats-io/nats-server/v2 in go.mod, L1 with a package main entry point at main.go, L14, so the standard go install github.com/nats-io/nats-server/v2@latest drops a single nats-server binary onto your path. Prebuilt binaries and Docker images are also published per release; the README itself is notably spare and points you to the official docs at docs.nats.io rather than embedding a quick start. Run the binary with no arguments and it listens for client connections on port 4222 — that default lives in code as DEFAULT_PORT, L78 and surfaces again in the CLI help, where usageStr, L27 documents -p, --port for clients and -m, --http_port for monitoring.

Because the protocol is plain text over TCP, you do not even need a client library to prove it works. telnet localhost 4222 greets you with an INFO line; send:

CONNECT {"verbose":false}
SUB inference.done 1

then from a second terminal:

PUB inference.done 11
hello world

and the first terminal prints MSG inference.done 1 11 followed by the payload. Those are not toy approximations — the exact OP_PUB, OP_SUB, and OP_MSG states of this protocol are enumerated in the parser starting at L75. For real applications, install the nats CLI and any of the 40+ client libraries, and the same subjects work unchanged. When you want durability, add a config file with jetstream: enabled and store_dir, pass it with -c, and Options.ProcessConfigFile, L1084 will validate everything before startup — changes to many settings can even be applied live through Server.Reload, L1438 without dropping connections.

The Read Loop: How a PUB Becomes a Fan-out

The elegance of the NATS server is that the hot path is almost embarrassingly direct. A connection’s readLoop, L1503 reads from the socket in growing buffers and feeds parse, L137, which keeps a per-client parse state and calls back into the client methods as operations complete. A CONNECT triggers processConnect, L2346, which authenticates the connection through checkAuthentication, L415 — supporting tokens, username/password, NKeys, and JWT-decoded accounts — and binds the client to its Account struct, L51.

Here is the trick that keeps routing fast: there is no global subscription table. Every account owns its own Sublist trie (the sl field at L70), so subject lookups stay cache-friendly and tenants cannot bloat each other’s match times. On publish, processPub, L3016 resolves the subject locally and processMsgResults, L5368 walks the matched subscription set, and for each target deliverMsg, L3854 appends the message to the subscriber’s outbound queue. Slow consumers are handled by capping those queues and, when a client falls too far behind, marking it a “slow consumer” rather than stalling the publisher — a deliberate choice that keeps the fast path lock-light and non-blocking.

JetStream: Streams, Consumers, and the File Store

Flipping on JetStream changes the story from “deliver and forget” to “store, replicate, and replay.” Streams are created over the same pub/sub fabric: a client publishes to $JS.API.STREAM.CREATE..., apiDispatch, L951 matches the request to a handler, and the stream registers an internal subscription so that ordinary publishes on its bound subjects land in processJetStreamMsg, L6486. There the engine applies de-duplication windows, per-stream limits (messages, bytes, age), and retention policy before calling into storage.

Storage behind JetStream is pluggable through the StreamStore interface, L95, with two in-tree implementations: memory (memStore.StoreMsg, L407) for ephemeral streams and the file store (StoreMsg, L5579) for durable ones. The file store is the crown jewel of this codebase — roughly fifteen thousand lines managing append-only message blocks with CRCs, optional at-rest encryption, async flush, and on-restart recovery, which is why a stream survives a crash or a rolling upgrade. Consumers read from that state: consumer.deliverMsg, L5895 sequences messages out to pull or push subscribers and tracks acknowledgements, so replaying from an arbitrary sequence is just re-walking the store. If you have followed our write-ups on log-structured systems like Loki, the shape will feel familiar — append-optimized blocks, coarse indexes, cheap sequential reads.

Clustering, Gateways, and Leaf Nodes

Single-server NATS is already useful, but the topology features are what make it fit AI deployments that sprawl across datacenters. Within a cluster, servers connect to each other as routes: startRouteAcceptLoop, L2738 accepts inbound route connections and addRoute, L2145 registers them. Discovery can be configured or gossip-style — servers announce themselves via processImplicitRoute, L1056 and relay new peer info with forwardNewRouteInfoToKnownServers, L1152, so you seed each node with a couple of addresses and the mesh self-assembles. Subscription interest propagates along routes so publishes traverse only links that actually lead to subscribers.

For JetStream itself, clustering means consensus: enabling it via enableJetStreamClustering, L1297 puts stream and consumer assignments under a Raft meta group, where Propose, L1048 replicates entries and elections pick the leader that owns each stream. Above clusters sit gateways — startGatewayAcceptLoop, L491 links independent clusters with interest-propagated messaging, useful for region-to-region fan-out. And below sit leaf nodes: startLeafNodeAcceptLoop, L1088 accepts edge servers, while a remote leaf dials home through connectToRemoteLeafNodeAsynchronously, L786. A leaf node keeps working when disconnected — your edge inference box keeps serving local subjects — and rejoins the hub later, which is exactly the model you want for a fleet of GPU nodes behind flaky links, à la Ray workers.

Monitoring the Server

Start the server with -m 8222 (the flag documented in main.go, L35) and you get an HTTP monitoring endpoint whose index is rendered by HandleRoot, L1523 — a deliberately plain HTML page listing the JSON endpoints. Varz, L1635 reports configuration and runtime stats, Connz, L205 lists live connections with their subscriptions and pending bytes, and Jsz, L3294 summarizes JetStream streams, consumers, and store usage. There is no built-in dashboard; the design assumption is that Prometheus scrapes these endpoints and Grafana draws the graphs — the same observability stack we described for OpenTelemetry-style setups. Beyond polling, the server emits system advisories on $SYS subjects via sendInternalMsg, L763, so connect events, account stats, and JetStream warnings can simply be subscribed to by an ops tool.

Honest Limits

NATS trades generality for focus, and it is worth being explicit about the edges. Core NATS is at-most-once: if a subscriber is slow or disconnected, it misses messages, period — JetStream is mandatory for anything you cannot afford to lose, and running it means managing store directories, block files, and cluster quorums. The README is famously minimal: no quick start, no benchmarks, no tuning guide — the real documentation lives on docs.nats.io. The monitoring story is JSON endpoints plus whatever dashboards you build yourself; do not expect a turnkey UI. JetStream’s Raft clustering adds operational surface — meta-group elections, peer cleanup, snapshot management — that a two-node setup will not teach you, so plan for at least three servers. And the subject-trie model rewards careful naming: wildcard-heavy subjects with low locality can pressure the match cache, so schema discipline matters more than it looks. Finally, production still wants TLS, JWT account boundaries, and resource limits configured thoughtfully — the code paths exist (checkAuthentication, L415 among them) but none are sensible defaults you can ignore.

None of that diminishes the core appeal: a ~15 MB Go binary that turns any VM, container, or Raspberry Pi into a messaging fabric with optional durability, honest clustering, and a protocol you can debug over telnet. For AI workloads built around fan-out inference, agent coordination, and event-driven data collection, NATS is often the smallest component that quietly carries the most traffic — and now you have the map of how it does it.

entry.title: Inside the OpenTelemetry Collector: The Go Engine That Routes Every Trace, Metric and Log

link.title: Inside the OpenTelemetry Collector: The Go Engine That Routes Every Trace, Metric and Log

entry.content:
Modern AI systems are telemetry furnaces. An LLM gateway emits metrics that classic web apps never had: tokens per second, time-to-first-token, queue depth per model replica, cache hit ratios on a prompt store. Every step of an agent — tool call, retrieval hit, retry — wants to be a span. GPU hosts want to report utilization, thermal events and batch occupancy as metrics, and the debugging session that starts with a hallucination usually ends with you reading traces at three in the morning. The hard part is not generating these signals; your frameworks already do. The hard part is moving them: different shapes, different backends, batching under bursty load, retries, tail sampling, redaction of prompts that may contain user data. That plumbing problem is exactly what the OpenTelemetry Collector was built to solve. Its README describes it plainly: a vendor-agnostic implementation of how to receive, process and export telemetry data — one binary that stands between your AI services and every backend you use, from Jaeger to Kafka to a managed vendor.

There are two repositories people conflate. open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector — the subject of this post — is the engine: the component interfaces, the OTLP-native data model, the config system, the service runtime that turns YAML into a directed graph of running components, and the otelcol binary itself. The sibling opentelemetry-collector-contrib repository is the long tail: hundreds of receivers, processors, exporters and connectors, from PostgreSQL scrapers to Kafka brokers. If you have ever added a component to a config file and wondered what actually happens next, the machinery lives in the core repo — and that is the machinery we are going to read, file by file, with line anchors into the main branch.

We will do it in two passes. The overview diagram below follows a signal from the command line to the exporter. The detail diagram then opens every stage up: the collector lifecycle, config resolution, the service graph internals, and the three pdata signal containers. Every symbol mentioned in the text links to the real source, verified in the repo as of today.

Figure 1 — The 10,000-meter view: the otelcol binary builds a Collector, which resolves configuration and hands component factories to the Service, which assembles a directed acyclic graph of receivers, processors and exporters that exchange pdata signals.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • NewCommand, L25 — the cobra root command is the binary’s front door; its RunE constructs a Collector and calls Run.
  • Collector struct, L100 — the process owner: settings, config provider, the Service, state and shutdown channels.
  • ConfigProvider.Get, L55 — serves the configuration on demand and on change.
  • Resolver.Resolve, L164 — fetches each config URI through a provider, merges the maps and expands references.
  • service.New, L108 — builds internal telemetry, extensions and the component graph.
  • graph.Build, L78 — turns the service config into a DAG of component instances.
  • receiverNode, L26 — one graph node per receiver instance, wired to the next consumers.
  • Traces, L21 — the pdata container every component actually passes around.

Figure 2 — The full plumbing: CLI and lifecycle, the confmap resolution stack, the service runtime, the data flow graph with its virtual nodes, and the pdata signal containers that carry your LLM metrics, agent spans and logs.

A Vendor-Agnostic Router, in One Binary

Everything starts in otelcol/. NewCommand, L25 assembles a cobra command whose RunE constructs NewCollector, L129 and then blocks in Collector.Run, L414. Command-line surface is deliberately tiny: flags.go registers the config flag, L15 — repeatable, one location per entry — plus a --set override flag at L39. Two diagnostic subcommands round it out: otelcol components (newComponentsCommand, L45) prints every factory baked into the binary from the Factories, L21 struct, and a validate subcommand (L13) checks a config without running it.

The Collector struct, L100 walks through four states, StateStarting through StateClosed (L30), and its Run method is just a startup call followed by a select loop: it waits on the config watcher (L464), on asynchronous component errors, on SIGHUP/SIGINT/SIGTERM, and on the channel closed by Collector.Shutdown, L166. Config change or reload signal triggers reloadConfiguration, L289, which tears down the retiring Service and builds a new one — with a partial-reload fast path (UpdateReceivers, L273) that restarts only the receivers that actually changed and leaves the rest of the graph untouched. For a long-running AI gateway this means you can tune processors without dropping in-flight signals.

The Config Layer: From a URI to a Struct

The Collector never reads files itself. ConfigProvider, L23 wraps a confmap.Resolver and exposes Get/Watch/Shutdown. Inside the resolver, Resolve, L164 retrieves each configured location through a pluggable Provider interface, L54, merges the resulting maps in order, runs converters, and expands references like ${env:OTEL_KEY}. The scheme dispatch is the elegant part: a file provider whose scheme is literally “file”, L18, an env provider, L21, plus http/https and yaml providers out of the box. Watching is symmetric: Resolver.Watch, L258 returns a channel that fires when any watched location changes.

The resolved map is unmarshalled into otelcol.Config, L22 — top-level maps for receivers, exporters, processors, connectors and extensions, plus the service section — and validated by Config.Validate, L49: an empty file is an error, at least one receiver and one exporter must be configured, and every component referenced by the service section must exist. Fail here and the process exits before any component is built.

The Service Graph: A DAG, Not a Chain

This is the part most people get wrong about the Collector. It is not a linear chain; it is a directed acyclic graph, assembled at runtime by the service/internal/graph package. service.New, L108 first creates the internal telemetry (resource, logger, meter and tracer providers), then calls initGraph, L340, which feeds builders and the configured signal flows into graph.Build, L78.

Build runs three phases. createNodes, L101 adds one node per component instance — receivers and exporters are deduplicated across flows of the same signal, processors are unique per flow, and connectors (connectorNode, L31) are type-checked so an exporter on one signal always pairs with a receiver on another. createEdges, L268 then wires each flow: receivers emit into a virtual capabilitiesNode, L20 that aggregates whether the flow mutates data, the processors are chained in config order, and a fanOutNode, L15 sits before the exporters so one signal can fan out to many backends. Finally buildComponents, L297 topologically sorts the graph (topo.Sort, L298) and instantiates real components in reverse order, handing each one its nextConsumers, L378 — this is the moment a receiver receives the consumer it will push spans into.

Startup respects the DAG: StartAll, L406 starts downstream components first so every consumer is ready before its producer (Service.Start, L232 starts extensions, then the graph, then logs the famous “Everything is ready” line), and ShutdownAll, L467 stops in the opposite order so components drain cleanly. The Host, L31 ties it together as the component.Host implementation, answering factory lookups (GetFactory, L48), status reporting and zPages.

From Install to Your First Model

From install to first flowing signal takes about five minutes, and it doubles as a working mental model of the whole machine — your first model of how telemetry moves.

  1. Download a distro binary. The README links the releases page, where the project publishes signed artifacts (cosign verification is documented in the README). Container images otel/opentelemetry-collector are published under the same release process.
  2. Write a minimal config. One OTLP receiver (gRPC on 4317, HTTP on 4318) and the debug exporter are the classic starting pair:
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318
exporters:
  debug:
    verbosity: detailed
service:
  telemetry:
    logs:
      level: info
  # under the service section you also declare your signal flows:
  # for each of traces, metrics and logs, list which receivers feed
  # which exporters, with optional processors between them.
  # The getting-started guide shows the exact stanza.
  1. Run it: otelcol --config=config.yaml. The config flag is the one requirement — command.go rejects a start without it, L61. For the precise service stanza, the official getting-started guide (linked from the README) walks through the exact flow declaration.
  2. Push one signal through. Any OTLP client will do — curl a JSON span to port 4318, or point a Python opentelemetry-sdk tracer at it. The debug exporter prints the pdata you just created, and you can literally watch your span travel receiver → capabilities node → fan-out → exporter, exactly as the diagram promised.

For an AI stack this scales up naturally: point your LLM gateway’s OTLP endpoint at the Collector, add a batch processor to absorb traffic spikes, and export metrics to Prometheus, traces to Jaeger, or mirror raw signals onto Kafka when a downstream consumer wants its own replay. Same binary, same graph, one config file.

pdata: Where Every Signal Lives

Every component in that graph speaks one in-memory language: pdata. The package doc says it directly — pdata defines the data model for all supported signals, L6. It is a hand-written Go mirror of the OTLP protobufs: Traces, L21 is a wrapper around resource-span slices (ResourceSpans, L49), Logs, L21 and Metrics, L21 follow the same resource → scope → record layering, and pcommon.Map, L18 with Range, L242 is the attribute bag they all share, alongside a fixed-size TraceID, L15. At the wire edge, ExportRequest, L17 wraps a Traces value for gRPC/HTTP transport without re-copying the data.

Why does a dedicated model matter? Because signals cross many component boundaries on their way through the graph, and re-serializing at each hop would be ruinous. pdata lets a receiver hand a mutable structure to a processor and on to an exporter with zero copies of the payload between them — but mutability is tracked: the capabilities node computes whether anything downstream mutates data, and the receiver side clones defensively when it does. When you build AI-specific processors (prompt redaction, token-cost attribution, trace sampling by latency), this is the API you write against, and the graph wiring is what guarantees your processor sees every signal exactly once.

Honest Limits

  • The core repo has no AI-specific components. Batching, tail sampling or prompt-scrubbing processors live in contrib (or in your own Go module). The core gives you the framework and a small stable set; the catalog is a separate dependency decision.
  • The service stanza is mandatory and strict. Validation requires at least one receiver and one exporter, and every reference must resolve — the empty-config errors are right there in config.go, L17.
  • The graph package is internal by design. You extend the Collector by implementing factories and components, not by editing the DAG; the flow shape is data-driven from config, which is a feature but also a constraint if you wanted exotic topologies.
  • The code moves fast. Every anchor in this post was verified against main on 2026-11-01; line numbers will drift, symbols less so. Treat the links as a snapshot.
  • No benchmarks here on purpose. The README’s own claims are qualitative — usable, performant, observable, extensible, unified — and I see no reason to invent numbers the project did not make.
  • Self-observability is real but easy to forget. The Host registers zPages endpoints (RegisterZPages, L110, rendering via HandleZPages, L21) that show the live graph and component status — turn them on before you need them at 3 a.m.

That is the whole journey: a cobra command, a config resolver, a graph builder, and a data model — four ideas that together route every trace, metric and log your AI stack will ever emit.

entry.title: Thanos: Giving Prometheus Unlimited Memory with Go and Object Storage

link.title: Thanos: Giving Prometheus Unlimited Memory with Go and Object Storage

entry.content:
If you run even a modest AI or ML fleet, your metrics outgrow your monitoring faster than your models outgrow your GPUs. A single GPU export loop that scrapes utilization, memory pressure, KV-cache occupancy and request latency every fifteen seconds generates millions of samples per series per year. Keep thirty days locally and every interesting question — what did peak inference latency look like during last quarter’s rollout, how did GPU thermal throttling drift across the summer, which experiment batch saturated the network — becomes unanswerable. Long-horizon telemetry is not a nice-to-have for machine learning systems; it is the training data for your capacity planning, your autoscaling rules and your postmortems.

Thanos exists for exactly this gap. The project describes itself as “a set of components that can be composed into a highly available metric system with unlimited storage capacity, which can be added seamlessly on top of existing Prometheus deployments.” It is a CNCF Incubating project written in Go, and its core trick is pragmatic: it keeps using the Prometheus 2.0 storage format — two-hour TSDB blocks — and simply makes those blocks durable in any object store, from S3 to MinIO, while layering on global querying, deduplication, downsampling and horizontal scaling.

What makes Thanos worth a source tour is that it is not one monolith but a constellation of small, composable processes, each with one job, all speaking one shared gRPC contract. In this post we walk the actual Go source — the block metadata model, the store gateway that serves bucket data, the compactor that rewrites history, the fan-out query layer, the rule evaluator and the stateless receive component that ingests remote writes — and map how they fit together. We read from the main branch of thanos-io/thanos throughout.

Overview: Prometheus sidecars and receive nodes push immutable blocks into object storage; the store gateway serves them via the Store API; the querier fans out across every endpoint behind a caching frontend; the compactor and ruler run as side operations.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything starts as one binary. The entrypoint in main, L44 describes itself as “a block storage based long-term storage for Prometheus”, and lines 56–63 register all eight subcommands — sidecar, store, query, rule, compact, tools, receive and query-frontend — so one Docker image covers the whole deployment.
  • The sidecar is the classic starting point. registerSidecar, L61 wires a process that sits next to Prometheus, proxies its data through the Store API, and when a bucket is configured, continuously uploads new TSDB blocks.
  • Uploads are handled by the shipper: Shipper.Sync, L344 scans the local data directory and pushes blocks into the bucket, while Shipper.upload, L478 does the actual transfer.
  • Every block is self-describing. The Meta, L66 struct carries the block’s ULID, min/max time, statistics and external labels — the glue that lets any component decide which block is relevant to a query.
  • On the serving side, the store gateway is BucketStore, L395: it syncs block metadata from the bucket and answers Series, L1560 requests by streaming chunks straight from object storage.
  • To keep the object store from melting under hot queries, index reads pass through CachingBucket, L39, which memoizes index and chunk-range reads in memory, memcached or Redis.
  • The query layer is where Thanos becomes “global”. EndpointSet, L255 tracks every Store API endpoint, and the fan-out querier around querier, L143 merges results from all of them in parallel, deduplicating replica pairs on the fly.
  • Two side processes keep history tidy and alerting global: the compactor, whose Syncer, L55 watches the bucket and rewrites overlapping blocks, and the ruler, whose Manager, L117 evaluates recording and alerting rules against the global view.

Detail view: the block fetcher and metadata model that all components share, the store gateway's lazy index readers and caching, the frontend's splitting and sharding tripperware, and the compactor's planner, downsampler and retention passes.

The Block Format That Everything Shares

The reason Thanos can scale is a data model choice, not a service mesh. Prometheus periodically cuts its head data into immutable, compressed two-hour blocks, each with a compact index and chunk files. Thanos treats those blocks as the unit of storage, replication and retention — upload them once and every other component only ever reads. The service Store, L26 definition in pkg/store/storepb/rpc.proto is the shared gRPC contract: a Series RPC that streams matching time series, plus LabelNames and LabelValues for discovery. Sidecars, store gateways and receive nodes all implement it, which is why the querier does not care whether data is twenty seconds old in a sidecar or five years old in a bucket.

Listing the bucket is consequently a critical path. NewMetaFetcher, L403 builds a concurrent metadata fetcher that lists block directories, downloads each meta.json, and passes it through a chain of filters — consistency delay, deletion marks, duplicate detection — before anyone trusts it. The store gateway then opens each block lazily: LazyBinaryReader, L70 memory-maps the index header only when a query actually touches that block, which is how a single gateway can serve terabytes without holding everything in RAM. Per-block series selection lives in the bucketBlock, L2431 machinery of pkg/store/bucket.go, with chunk readers that fetch and decompress on demand.

From Install to Your First Global Query

The fastest verified path uses the official image published at quay.io/thanos/thanos on every commit to main, with minor releases every six weeks. Assume Prometheus is already running locally and you have a bucket config file for your object store — S3, GCS, Azure or MinIO all work through the same YAML shape.

First, attach a sidecar to Prometheus and start backing data up:

thanos sidecar \
    --tsdb.path            /var/prometheus \
    --prometheus.url       "http://localhost:9090" \
    --objstore.config-file bucket_config.yaml

That command, straight from the project’s quick tutorial, ships every new block to the bucket and simultaneously exposes a Store API on port 19090 backed by the live Prometheus data. Give every Prometheus instance a globally unique set of external labels (for example replica: A on one and replica: B on its HA twin) — this is mandatory, because those labels are how data from different instances is later told apart and merged.

Next, point a stateless querier at all your Store API endpoints:

thanos query \
    --http-address 0.0.0.0:19192 \
    --endpoint     1.2.3.4:19090 \
    --endpoint     1.2.3.5:19090 \
    --endpoint     dnssrv+_grpc._tcp.thanos-store.monitoring.svc

Endpoints can be static, DNS A records (dns+) or SRV records (dnssrv+). Open the UI on port 19192 and you can run one PromQL query across every connected Prometheus at once; add --query.replica-label replica and the querier transparently deduplicates the HA pairs. Because the querier implements the Prometheus HTTP API, Grafana can point at it unchanged. Once your historical data is in the bucket, run a store gateway (thanos store --data-dir /var/thanos/store --objstore.config-file bucket_config.yaml), register its endpoint the same way, and years of data appear in the same query. Finally, a singleton compactor (thanos compact --data-dir /var/thanos/compact --objstore.config-file bucket_config.yaml) keeps the bucket compacted and downsampled. For Kubernetes fleets, the kube-thanos manifests and the Prometheus Operator integration package all of this into standard workloads.

Compaction, Downsampling and Retention

Blocks in a bucket do not compact themselves. The compactor is a single-instance process that periodically lists the bucket with the same MetaFetcher, L712 machinery as everyone else, groups overlapping blocks by their external labels, and rewrites each group into progressively larger time ranges. The rewrite itself is delegated to a second-generation engine: Compactor.WriteSeries, L77 in pkg/compactv2 merges overlapping block contents through a streaming series writer, while the tsdbBasedPlanner, L23 decides which blocks are due for the next compaction level.

Two extra passes make long histories queryable. The downsampler builds coarse 5-minute and 1-hour resolutions of every block — Downsample, L73 aggregates raw chunks into counters-with-resets and averaged histograms — and the query layer automatically picks a resolution matching the step of your query. Retention is symmetric: ApplyRetentionPolicyByResolution, L25 marks blocks whose max time falls outside the configured window for each resolution, and the BlocksCleaner, L26 physically deletes marked blocks from the bucket. The result is a storage hierarchy where a year-long dashboard hits 1h-downsampled data while a five-minute incident review hits raw blocks.

Ingestion at Scale with Receive

Sidecars are perfect when Prometheus owns the data, but what if you need to push telemetry in — from federated clusters, from jobs that speak the remote-write protocol, from other remote-write compatible sources? The receive component is a stateless, horizontally scalable ingestion tier. Incoming writes hit Handler, L142, which validates and routes each request through a Hashring, L60 — a consistent-hash ring over receive nodes — so every tenant’s series lands on exactly one responsible node, with configurable replication factor fanning copies to peers.

The responsible node appends through Writer.Write, L74 into one of several local TSDBs owned by MultiTSDB, L55, a storage multiplexer that isolates tenants and uploads each tenant’s blocks to the bucket via its own shipper. Because every receive node also exposes the Store API, the querier sees ingested data the same way it sees sidecar data — no special casing anywhere in the query path. If you already push samples into Prometheus remote write, receive is a drop-in escalation path from single-instance to distributed ingestion.

Honest Limits

Thanos is infrastructure, not magic, and the sharp edges are worth naming before you deploy it:

  • Compactor is a singleton by design. The documentation is explicit that it must run as a single instance and must not run concurrently with manual bucket modifications; two compactors racing over the same bucket is the classic operational footgun.
  • Global queries are only as fast as their slowest endpoint. The fan-out querier merges responses in parallel, but one misbehaving store gateway or sidecar inflates every cross-cluster query. Partial response strategies exist, but they trade completeness for latency.
  • Query cost grows with label cardinality, not just time range. Downsampling makes long-range dashboards cheap, but high-cardinality series still dominate index lookups; sharding and frontend caching (NewTripperware, L37) mitigate rather than eliminate this.
  • External labels are load-bearing. A collision between two Prometheus instances’ external labels leads to overlapping blocks in the bucket, and untangling that is painful. Set them before the first upload, not after.
  • The object store is now a production dependency. Latency and rate limits of your bucket tier propagate into query latencies; budget a real storage backend rather than treating it as cold archive.

For teams that want object-storage-backed metrics without a component zoo, alternatives like VictoriaMetrics take a more monolithic route — we compared that trade-off in our VictoriaMetrics source tour. For Kubernetes-native fleets that already run Prometheus sidecars, though, Thanos’s block-first design in about a hundred thousand lines of Go remains the reference architecture for “query any window, any replica, one PromQL”.

entry.title: Valkey Source Tour: How the Community-Governed Redis Fork Rewired Its Core

link.title: Valkey Source Tour: How the Community-Governed Redis Fork Rewired Its Core

entry.content:
In March 2024 the Redis project moved its source tree to a source-available license, and the open-source world responded the way open-source worlds do: it forked. The result is Valkey, a high-performance data structure server that, per its own README, “was forked from the open source Redis project right before the transition to their new source available licenses.” The code stayed under a 3-clause BSD license — the COPYING file carries a joint notice: “Copyright (c) 2024-present, Valkey contributors” alongside “Copyright (c) 2006-2020, Redis Ltd.” What makes Valkey more than a rebranded snapshot is governance: the project is a Series of LF Projects, LLC under the Linux Foundation umbrella, and its GOVERNANCE.md establishes a Technical Steering Committee with an unusual safeguard — no more than one third of TSC members may be employees or representatives of the same organization. That single rule is the design answer to “what stops one vendor from capturing the project,” and it is written into the repository, not a press release.

Technically, Valkey remains exactly what ML and backend engineers reach for daily: a C-based, in-memory data structure server speaking RESP over TCP, with strings, hashes, sorted sets, streams, pub/sub, and the rest of the vocabulary you already know. For AI workloads it slots naturally into the boring-but-critical roles — embedding cache, session store, rate limiter, feature store, and now even LLM prefix reuse, because Valkey shipped a purpose-built path-hash data type (PHSET, PHGET, PHLONGEST) designed for path-shaped keys like token prefix trees. The mental model from caching layers in front of a FastAPI service transfers directly: keys in, keys out, sub-millisecond.

But here is the interesting part for this tour. We previously walked the Redis source code on this site, and if you diff the two codebases at the file level, the fork has genuinely diverged. dict.c — the hash table heart of Redis for fifteen years — is now hashtable.c. Async IO threading, once sprinkled across networking.c, got its own file, io_threads.c. Replication grew a dual-channel mode that Redis does not have, and slot migration in cluster mode was rebuilt around a job state machine in cluster_migrateslots.c. This post is the Valkey angle: what the community did with the codebase once it owned it. Every symbol and line number below was verified against the unstable branch at commit 3ef5fef19fe4, so the anchors may drift as the tree moves — that is the price of touring a living branch.

Overview: one request flowing through Valkey — boot and event loop on the left, the async IO layer, command dispatch across the data types, the hashtable-backed keyspace, and the persistence and replication paths on the right. Generated from valkey-io/valkey at unstable.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Boot and loop. main(), L7935 initializes config (initServerConfig), opens listeners via initServer, then enters aeMain, L689 — the same epoll/kqueue/select event-loop family Valkey inherited, with serverCron, L1601 running as a timed job on that loop.
  • Networking. readQueryFromClient, L4893 parses RESP into the query buffer. Note the signature: it now takes a connection *, part of a small ABI drift from Redis, and replies drain through writeToClient, L3569, whose return type changed from void to int.
  • The headline: IO threads. trySendReadToIOThreads, L693 and trySendWriteToIOThreads, L742 hand socket reads and writes to worker threads; the main thread harvests results in processIOThreadsResponses, L1324. Even cluster link traffic gets the treatment.
  • Dispatch. processCommand, L4647 resolves commands from a table generated out of declarative src/commands/*.json specs, checks ACLs, and dispatches.
  • Data types. setCommand, L265 for the string hot path, zaddGenericCommand, L1226 for ranked data, and the fork’s newest addition, phsetCommand, L230, the path-hash type.
  • Keyspace. lookupKey, L87 is the single chokepoint every command passes, backed by the renamed engine: hashtableCreate, L1266.
  • Persistence. rdbSaveBackground, L1864 forks to snapshot; flushAppendOnlyFile, L1184 fsyncs the log from beforeSleep.
  • Replication. syncCommand, L1412 serves SYNC/PSYNC and negotiates the dual-channel capability flag, while feedReplicationBuffer shares one replication stream with all replicas.

The detail view: 34 nodes across boot, async IO, data types, storage engine, persistence, replication, and cluster — every edge labeled with the symbol that drives it, anchored to valkey-io/valkey at unstable.

What Actually Changed After the Fork

The license story gets the headlines, but the code tells you what priorities the new maintainers set. The clearest structural statement is src/io_threads.c itself. In Redis, the IO-threading logic lived inside networking.c, which at several thousand lines already carried client state, RESP parsing, output buffers, and more. Valkey’s maintainers carved the entire async machinery into a dedicated file with a coherent surface: initIOThreads at L599 spawns the workers, trySendReadToIOThreads and trySendWriteToIOThreads enqueue jobs, processIOThreadsResponses at L1324 applies finished work back on the main thread, and waitForClientIO keeps blocking operations correct when a client’s IO is still in flight. The io-threads config at config.c L3568 is marked MODIFIABLE_CONFIG, meaning you can tune worker count at runtime without a restart — a genuine operational upgrade for workloads whose traffic shape changes across the day.

The storage layer got the same treatment. Redis’s dict.c became hashtable.c, and the naming is honest about scope: hashtableCreate at L1266 and the hashtable API are now the substrate, with kvstore.c on top managing the per-database containers and accounting (kvstoreMemUsage at L378). Even expire.c drifted: activeExpireCycle at L466 now returns ustime_t instead of void, reporting back how long the cycle ran. Individually these are small things; together they read as a team that treats the codebase as theirs to keep improving rather than a shrine.

From Install to Your First Model

Valkey builds the old-fashioned way, which is to say it just works. Clone the repository and run make — that produces src/valkey-server and src/valkey-cli, exactly as the README describes. The build system exposes the usual toggles: make BUILD_TLS=yes for in-process TLS (or BUILD_TLS=module to load it as a module instead), and an experimental RDMA transport via make BUILD_RDMA=yes, which is Linux-only and, per the README, “may be changed or removed in any minor or major version.” Zstandard support for RDB streaming and replication compression is opt-in with BUILD_ZSTD=yes. There is also a newer, explicitly experimental CMake build for people who want IDE integration through compile_commands.json. On Linux the default allocator is jemalloc, chosen (as the README notes) for its fragmentation behavior; a MALLOC=libc override exists when you need it. Before trusting the build, the README recommends make test, with dedicated suites available as make test-unit, make test-cluster, make test-sentinel, and make test-modules.

Then the first run is two commands. Start the server:

cd src
./valkey-server

and from another terminal:

./valkey-cli
valkey> ping
PONG
valkey> set foo bar
OK
valkey> get foo
"bar"
valkey> incr mycounter
(integer) 1

That transcript is lifted straight from the README, and it is the whole onboarding story. From there, the AI-shaped uses fall out of the data types: a string key per embedding with a TTL gives you a cache-aside embedding store; a hash per user holds session state; a sorted set (ZADD/ZRANGE) is a leaderboard or a time-ordered feature queue; and the path-hash type exists precisely because LLM inference started asking for “longest known prefix of this token path” queries — PHSET and PHLONGEST at L458 implement exactly that. For load testing your setup, the repo ships valkey-benchmark (its main() lives at L2386 in src/valkey-benchmark.c), so you can measure on your own hardware instead of trusting anyone’s blog numbers — including ours. One compatibility note worth knowing before you script anything: make install creates redis-server and redis-cli symlinks pointing at the Valkey binaries, so old tooling keeps working, and USE_REDIS_SYMLINKS=no skips that if you want a clean namespace.

Dual-Channel Replication and the Cluster Work

Replication is where Valkey’s biggest protocol-level bet lives. Classic Redis replication sends the RDB snapshot and the live command stream over the same connection, which means the replica cannot reliably process commands until the snapshot finishes transferring — the stream would interleave with the bulk payload. Valkey’s dual-channel mode lets a replica open a second connection so the RDB flows over one channel while replication commands flow over the other. In the code, the replica advertises a dual-channel capability during PSYNC (parsed at replication.c L1800, with the capability bit set at L1510), the RDB-loading path tracks a distinct REPL_DUAL_CHANNEL_RDB_LOAD state in rdb.c, and even the background-IO worker carries an is_dual_channel flag at bio.c L140 so cleanup knows which connection set it is tearing down. It is opt-in through the dual-channel-replication-enabled config at config.c L3463, and disabled by default — a conservative rollout for a change that touches the most dangerous code path in the system.

Cluster mode got two quieter but telling upgrades. The slot-migration machinery in cluster_migrateslots.c is a new file implementing slot export/import as explicit job objects with a state machine (connectSlotExportJob at L104), replacing the older synchronous MIGRATE-key-by-key flow — resumable, observable migrations instead of long brittle moves. And cluster_slot_stats.c adds per-slot traffic accounting surfaced through CLUSTER SLOT-STATS (collectAndSortSlotStats at L82), so operators can finally see which of the 16384 slots are hot before deciding how to rebalance, rather than guessing. The heartbeat of it all remains clusterCron, L6908 in cluster_legacy.c, running gossip, failover, and link upkeep — the “legacy” suffix is a naming choice for the classic cluster implementation, not a deprecation notice.

Honest Limits

Touring a living branch has a shelf life: everything above was verified against unstable at commit 3ef5fef19fe4, and Valkey does not treat unstable as a stable API — line numbers, and occasionally file homes, will move. The marquee features are young: dual-channel replication ships disabled by default, the RDMA transport is explicitly experimental and Linux-only, and the CMake build is labeled experimental alongside the long-standing Makefile build. The path-hash commands are new enough that client library support outside the mainline clients should be checked before you design around them. And while the BSD license plus symlink compatibility make Valkey a low-friction Redis stand-in for servers and clients, the module ecosystem is a separate compatibility surface — extensions written against Redis module APIs need testing rather than assuming. Finally, keep the durability story honest with yourself: this is still an in-memory database. AOF with everysec fsync via flushAppendOnlyFile bounds your loss window but does not eliminate it; if you need stronger durability guarantees for a subset of data, put it in something built for that — a MinIO bucket for artifacts, or a coordination-grade store like etcd for small state where consensus matters more than latency. Valkey pairs with those; it does not replace them. A useful framing: Valkey for hot, small, latency-critical state; Kafka for durable event history; MinIO for bytes at rest.

That combination is why the fork matters for AI infrastructure specifically. Model serving stacks lean heavily on the cache-session-feature triad, and Valkey’s trajectory — runtime-tunable IO threading, dual-channel replication cutting failover time, slot-level observability, prefix-reuse primitives — reads like a wishlist gathered from exactly those deployments. The codebase is C, the license is BSD-3, the governance caps any single vendor at one third of the TSC, and the event loop is still the one you know. The fork did not just survive the split; it started paying rent.
